# Vendored NIST CAVP test vectors — provenance

These files are **verbatim copies** of the NIST Cryptographic Algorithm Validation
Program (CAVP) Secure Hash Standard byte-oriented test vectors. They are the
published-answer half of `../kat_published.rs`; nothing in this directory was
generated by this repository.

## Files kept, and their SHA-256

Computed with `shasum -a 256` (OpenSSL), **not** with `trust-sha2`. The same
values are pinned in `kat_published.rs::CAVP_FILE_DIGESTS`, where they are
re-checked on every test run so a silently edited or truncated vector file fails
loudly instead of quietly shrinking the KAT set.

## Why these six and not the rest of the archive

The `ShortMsg` files are what make the **padding-boundary** vectors *published*
rather than self-generated. FIPS 180-4 §5.1 makes the digest a function of the
message length, and the interesting lengths are where the padding decision
changes — `len mod 64 == 55/56` for SHA-224/256 and `len mod 128 == 111/112` for
SHA-384/512. The `ShortMsg` files carry **every** byte length from 0 to one full
block (64 / 128), contiguously, so every one of those transitions is covered by a
NIST-published answer with no interpolation.

The `Monte` files are the CAVS Monte Carlo chained test: 100 checkpoints, each
1000 iterations of `MD[i] = SHA(MD[i-3] || MD[i-2] || MD[i-1])`. That is 100,000
dependent hashes per algorithm — the only vector here that would catch a state
carry-over defect that a one-shot digest cannot see.

`LongMsg.rsp` (1.7 MB each) and the `Monte.txt` intermediate-value files were
**not** vendored: 3.4 MB of data for coverage that `tests/differential_sha2.rs`
(every length 0..600, plus a 1,000,003-byte input) and the FIPS 180-4
1,000,000-`'a'` vector already provide. SHA-1, SHA-512/224 and SHA-512/256 are
not implemented by this crate.

## Independent corroboration performed at vendoring time

Every record in all six files was recomputed with CPython 3.9 `hashlib`
(OpenSSL) before the files were committed — 388 `ShortMsg` records and 200 Monte
checkpoints (200,000 chained hashes). **Zero mismatches.** So these files are not
merely "what NIST published"; they are a point where NIST and OpenSSL agree, and
`kat_published.rs` then asks whether `trust-sha2` joins them.
